[L1] Data Abstraction
[L2] 
[L3] Consider the difference between Listing 6-1 and Listing 6-2. Both represent
[L4] the data of a point on the Cartesian plane. And yet one exposes its
[L5] implementation and the other completely hides it.
[L6] 
[L7] Listing 6-1 Concrete Point
[L8]    public class Point {
[L9]      public double x;
[L10]      public double y;
[L11]    }
[L12] 
[L13] Listing 6-2 Abstract Point
[L14]    public interface Point {
[L15]      double getX();
[L16]      double getY();
[L17]      void setCartesian(double x, double y);
[L18]      double getR();
[L19]      double getTheta();
[L20]      void setPolar(double r, double theta);
[L21]    }
[L22] 
[L23] The beautiful thing about Listing 6-2 is that there is no way you can tell
[L24] whether the implementation is in rectangular or polar coordinates. It might
[L25] be neither! And yet the interface still unmistakably represents a data
[L26] structure.
[L27] 
[L28] But it represents more than just a data structure. The methods enforce an
[L29] access policy. You can read the individual coordinates independently, but
[L30] you must set the coordinates together as an atomic operation.
[L31] 
[L32] Listing 6-1, on the other hand, is very clearly implemented in rectangular
[L33] coordinates, and it forces us to manipulate those coordinates independently.
[L34] This exposes implementation. Indeed, it would expose implementation even
[L35] if the variables were private and we were using single variable getters and
[L36] setters.
[L37] 
[L38] Hiding implementation is not just a matter of putting a layer of functions
[L39] between the variables. Hiding implementation is about abstractions! A class
[L40] does not simply push its variables out through getters and setters. Rather it
[L41] exposes abstract interfaces that allow its users to manipulate the essence of
[L42] the data, without having to know its implementation.
[L43] 
[L44] 
[L45] 
[L46] Consider Listing 6-3 and Listing 6-4. The first uses concrete terms to
[L47] communicate the fuel level of a vehicle, whereas the second does so with
[L48] the abstraction of percentage. In the concrete case you can be pretty sure
[L49] that these are just accessors of variables. In the abstract case you have no
[L50] clue at all about the form of the data.
[L51] 
[L52] Listing 6-3 Concrete Vehicle
[L53]    public interface Vehicle {
[L54]      double getFuelTankCapacityInGallons();
[L55]      double getGallonsOfGasoline();
[L56]    }
[L57] 
[L58] Listing 6-4 Abstract Vehicle
[L59]    public interface Vehicle {
[L60]      double getPercentFuelRemaining();
[L61]    }
[L62] 
[L63] In both of the above cases the second option is preferable. We do not want
[L64] to expose the details of our data. Rather we want to express our data in
[L65] abstract terms. This is not merely accomplished by using interfaces and/or
[L66] getters and setters. Serious thought needs to be put into the best way to
[L67] represent the data that an object contains. The worst option is to blithely
[L68] add getters and setters.
[L69] 
[L70] 
[L71] 
[L72] Data/Object Anti-Symmetry
[L73] 
[L74] These two examples show the difference between objects and data
[L75] structures. Objects hide their data behind abstractions and expose functions
[L76] that operate on that data. Data structure expose their data and have no
[L77] meaningful functions. Go back and read that again. Notice the
[L78] complimentary nature of the two definitions. They are virtual opposites.
[L79] This difference may seem trivial, but it has far-reaching implications.
[L80] 
[L81] Consider, for example, the procedural shape example in Listing 6-5. The
[L82] Geometry class operates on the three shape classes. The shape classes are simple
[L83] data structures without any behavior. All the behavior is in the Geometry class.

[L20] G6: Code at Wrong Level of Abstraction
[L21] 
[L22] It is important to create abstractions that separate higher level general
[L23] concepts from lower level detailed concepts. Sometimes we do this by
[L24] creating abstract classes to hold the higher level concepts and derivatives to
[L25] hold the lower level concepts. When we do this, we need to make sure that
[L26] the separation is complete. We want all the lower level concepts to be in the
[L27] derivatives and all the higher level concepts to be in the base class.
[L28] 
[L29] For example, constants, variables, or utility functions that pertain only to
[L30] the detailed implementation should not be present in the base class. The
[L31] base class should know nothing about them.
[L32] 
[L33] This rule also pertains to source files, components, and modules. Good
[L34] software design requires that we separate concepts at different levels and
[L35] place them in different containers. Sometimes these containers are base
[L36] classes or derivatives and sometimes they are source files, modules, or
[L37] 
[L38]

[L41] complete. We don’t want lower and higher level concepts mixed together.

parts:
The snippet you’ve pasted does three things in `setupSignalRConnection()`:

1. **Logs the configuration step**  
   ```kotlin
   Timber.i("SignalRTrackingService: configuring HubConnection")
   ```  
   This writes an INFO-level message to Logcat (or any other planted Timber trees) so you can see when your service is about to build its SignalR connection.

2. **Creates a `HubConnection` pointing at your hub URL**  
   ```kotlin
   hubConnection = HubConnectionBuilder
     .create(hubUrl)
     …
     .build()
   ```  
   Under the covers this prepares all the plumbing needed to talk to your SignalR server over WebSockets (or Long Polling, depending on transport negotiation).

3. **Tells SignalR to automatically reconnect using your custom back-off schedule**  
   ```kotlin
   .withAutomaticReconnect { context ->
     // context.previousRetryCount is 0 on the first failure, 1 on the second, etc.
     val idx = context.previousRetryCount
       .coerceAtMost(retryTimes.size - 1)
     retryTimes[idx]
   }
   ```  
   - **`retryTimes`** is your predefined list of delays, e.g. `[1_000L, 2_000L, 5_000L, 10_000L]`.  
   - On each disconnection, SignalR will wait the number of milliseconds you return from this lambda before trying to re-establish the connection.  
   - By using `previousRetryCount.coerceAtMost(retryTimes.size – 1)`, you ensure that once you exhaust your list of delays, SignalR keeps using the last (longest) delay for all subsequent attempts.

Together, this means your service will:

- Log that it’s configuring the connection.  
- Build a `HubConnection` against `hubUrl`.  
- Whenever that connection drops, automatically try to reconnect after 1 s on the first failure, 2 s on the second, 5 s on the third, 10 s on the fourth—and thereafter continue retrying every 10 s until it succeeds.
